_comment: Used by the Windows Triage Decision Tree (Module 3) and the family dropdown in the DFIR Report Builder (Module 5). To add a family: append an object below with a unique id, a name, an 'indicators' array using only ids that exist in indicator-groups.json, a one/two-sentence scope note, a suggested next step, and a 'source' citation verified against the publisher's own site. No JS changes needed -- both widgets read this file at load time.

families.name: DeadLock
families.scope: Rust-based encryptor deployed by multiple affiliates, including Lynx/INC-linked actors. Recovery infrastructure resolves via a Polygon smart contract plus the Session messenger — a single-endpoint takedown will not fully disrupt victim communications.
families.response: Prioritize memory capture before process exit (Module 5). Check drive roots for RECOVERY_CHAT.<uid>.html. Treat disabled event channels as a hunting signal even without explicit log entries.

source.title: Microsoft Security Blog — DeadLock ransomware technical breakdown

families.name: The Gentlemen
families.scope: Go-based ransomware-as-a-service tracked by Microsoft as Storm-2697, distinguished from most peers by aggressive self-propagation — it spreads across a network on its own rather than needing to be deployed host by host.
families.response: Treat this as a network-wide incident from the first host found, not a single-machine one. Prioritize credential rotation and segmentation alongside triage. Check Fortinet FortiGate and VPN patch levels for the initial access point.

source.title: Microsoft Security Blog — The Gentlemen ransomware: dissecting a self-propagating Go encryptor

families.name: LockBit-pattern (documented RaaS TTPs)
families.scope: A widely documented affiliate/RaaS pattern built around intermittent encryption for speed. Referenced here as a documented TTP set for pattern-matching, not a claim about current operational status.
families.response: Confirm intermittent-encryption striping with full-length entropy scanning, not a header-only check. Correlate affiliate tooling against known IOC sets before attributing.

source.title: CISA AA23-165A — Understanding Ransomware Threat Actors: LockBit

families.name: BlackCat/ALPHV-pattern
families.scope: One of the earliest major Rust-based RaaS families, notable for a highly configurable JSON-driven encryption mode (full/fast/adaptive).
families.response: Recover and parse any dropped configuration artifact — encryption mode selection is often logged there and materially changes recoverability odds.

families.name: Akira-pattern
families.scope: Frequently associated with VPN-based initial access; Windows and Linux/ESXi-targeting variants have been documented.
families.response: Check edge VPN/remote-access logs first for initial access; confirm whether an ESXi-targeting variant is in scope if virtualization hosts were affected.

families.name: Play/PlayCrypt-pattern
families.scope: Block-splitting intermittent encryption; initial access frequently tied to exploited public-facing applications.
families.response: Audit internet-facing application and edge-device patch levels as a priority access-vector line of inquiry.

families.name: Qilin-pattern
families.scope: Documented in both Rust and Go variants under an affiliate/RaaS structure.
families.response: Early binary language identification (Rust vs. Go build artifacts) helps route the rest of the reverse-engineering effort.

source.title: CIS/MS-ISAC — Qilin: Top Ransomware Threat to SLTTs in Q2 2025
source.note: No dedicated joint CISA advisory as of last check; this is the closest equivalent source.
